_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 162 - Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes chs. 18 & 20 (Keoua's army, Kapiolani) and Legends of Ma-ui (Gutenberg #32601, 1910): chs. 3 (lifting the sky), 7 (Tuna), 8 (brother-in-law NZ variants), 9 (kite-flying), 12 (Hina of Hilo). Topics 3 heroic, 9 sacred landscape, 11 taboo. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Pele Destroys Keoua's Army at Kilauea, 1790
title.zh: 一七九〇年佩蕾滅凱瓦阿軍

region.zh: 夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山口旁通道

texts.period: Historical eruption of November 1790; recorded by Dibble (1839) and Kamakau (Kuokoa 1867)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (Chicago 1916), quoting Dibble and Kamakau

summary.en: Fleeing Kamehameha, the chief Keoua marches his army past Kilauea in three companies. A column of fire blazes higher than Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa, sand and ashes and great stones falling for days; the rear company, hurrying forward rejoicing at their escape, finds the central division all corpses - some lying, some sitting upright clasping wives and children and pressing noses in a final farewell, so lifelike that only touch proved them dead. A solitary hog alone survived. The people said Pele had taken Kamehameha under her protection.
summary.zh: 凱瓦阿為避卡美哈梅哈，率軍分三隊經基拉韋厄而行。火山噴出高過兩座大山的火柱，沙石灰石連日落降數日；殿後部隊慶幸脫險趕上前隊，卻見中路全軍已成屍骸——或臥或坐，有人還緊抱妻兒、鼻息相觸作永訣，栩栩如生，觸之方知已死；全隊唯餘孤豚一口生還。民間皆言：佩蕾已將卡美哈梅哈納入她的護佑。

sensitivity.note: Historic eruption read through Pele-worship; the Kilauea military fatality of 1790 is documented.

passages.text: Almost exactly thirty-four years before Kapiolani defied the worship of the fire-goddess Pele, Keoua, a high chief, lost a large part of his army near the volcano Kilauea. This was in November, 1790. Ka-lani-opuu had been king over the island Hawaii; when he died in 1782 he left the kingdom to his son Kiwalao, giving the second place to his nephew Kamehameha. War soon arose between the cousins; Kamehameha defeated and killed the young king, and Kiwalao's half-brother Keoua escaped to his district Kau. For some years the three factions practically let each other alone, although there was desultory fighting; then Keoua attacked Hilo, killed his uncle and ravaged Kamehameha's lands along the northeastern side of the island. Kamehameha quickly returned from Maui and made an immediate attack on his enemy; the chief was defeated and driven through forests along the eastern side of Mauna Kea to Hilo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Keoua heard of an attack on his home district, gave the fish-ponds and fertile lands of Hilo to some of his chiefs, and hastened to cross the island with his army by way of a path near the volcano Kilauea, dividing his warriors into three parties and taking charge of the first in person. They passed the crater at a time of great volcanic activity. A native writer, probably Kamakau, in the native newspaper Kuokoa, 1867, describes the destruction of the central part of this army by an awful explosion from Kilauea: 'Thus was it done. Sand, ashes, and stones grew up from the pit into a very high column of fire, standing straight up. The mountains of Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa were below it. The people even from Ka-wai-hae saw this wonderful column with fire glowing and blazing to its very top. When this column became great it blew all to pieces into sand and ashes and great stones, which for some days continued to fall around the sides of Kilauea. Men, women, and children were killed. Mona, one of the army, who saw all this but who escaped, said that one of the chiefesses was ill and some hundreds of the army had delayed their journey to guard her and so escaped this death.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916), quoting Kamakau; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dibble, the first among the missionaries to prepare a history of the islands, gave the following description of the event: 'The army of Keoua set out on their way in three different companies. The company in advance had not proceeded far before the ground began to shake and rock beneath their feet, and it became quite impossible to stand. Soon a dense cloud of darkness was seen to rise out of the crater, and almost at the same instant the electrical effect upon the air was so great that the thunder began to roar in the heavens and the lightning to flash; the whole region was enveloped and the light of day was entirely excluded. Soon followed an immense volume of sand and cinders which were thrown in high heaven and came down in a destructive shower for many miles around; some few persons of the forward company were burned to death by the sand and cinders and others were seriously injured. The rear body, which was nearest the volcano at the time of the eruption, seemed to suffer the least injury, and after the earthquake and shower of sand had passed over hastened forward to escape the dangers which threatened them. But what was their surprise and consternation when, on coming up with their comrades of the centre party, they discovered them all to have become corpses. Some were lying down, and others sitting upright clasping with dying grasp their wives and children and joining noses (their form of expressing affection) as in the act of taking a final leave. So much like life they looked that they at first supposed them merely at rest, and it was not until they had come up to them and handled them that they could detect their mistake. Of the whole party, including women and children, not one of them survived to relate the catastrophe that had befallen their comrades; the only living being they found was a solitary hog, in company with one of the families which had been so suddenly bereft of life.' Keoua's prophets ascribed this blow from the gods to their high chief's gift of the fish-ponds, considered the favorite food-producers for offerings to Hiiaka, the youngest member of the Pele family. Kamehameha's prophets said this eruption was the favor of the gods on his temple building, and the people said it was proof that Pele had taken Kamehameha under her especial protection.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 18 (1916), quoting Dibble; not verbatim.

title.en: Kapiolani Defies the Goddess of Kilauea, 1824
title.zh: 一八二四年卡皮歐拉尼挑戰火山女神

region.zh: 夏威夷島基拉韋厄火山口邊

texts.period: Historical event of December 1824; recorded by Richards, Bingham and Alexander (19th c.)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (Chicago 1916), quoting Richards, Bingham and Alexander

summary.en: Kapiolani, wife of the orator-chief Naihe, walks a hundred miles over sharp lava to Kilauea to break the worship of Pele. A rival priestess mumbles a 'letter from Pele'; Kapiolani reads back from her own book. At the crater's brink the berry-feeder warns 'You will die by Pele'; she answers 'I shall not die by your god; that fire was kindled by my God', descends several hundred feet, eats the consecrated ohelo berries, throws stones into the fire-pit, and prays. 'All the people saw that she was not injured and pronounced Pele to be powerless.'
summary.zh: 演說家酋長奈伊希之妻卡皮歐拉尼徒步百里，踏過鋒利熔岩前往基拉韋厄，誓破佩蕾之祀。途中女祭司展『佩蕾之信』喃喃咒罵；卡皮歐拉尼便朗讀自己識字課本中的經文相答。火山口畔，奉食者勸阻：『你必死於佩蕾。』她答：『我不會死於你們的神；這火是我神所點燃的。』她下行數百呎，食聖莓、擲石入火坑、同禱而返——『全境之民親見她毫髮無傷，皆稱佩蕾已無權能。』

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era event; retained as the historical end-point of Pele worship. Recorded with its Christian sources noted.

passages.text: The story of the high chiefess Kapiolani and her conflict with Pele, the goddess of Kilauea, in December, 1824, is historic. Kapiolani was the daughter of Keawe-mau-hili, the high chief of the district of Hilo. She became a tall, portly woman, with keen black eyes and an engaging countenance, a queen in appearance when with other chiefs or chiefesses; she was the wife of Na-ihe, the high chief of the district of Kona, said to be the national orator or best speaker on government affairs among the chiefs. Kapiolani, the-bending-arch-of-heaven, was very intelligent, quick-witted and fearless; both were so influential that they were chosen by Kamehameha as members of his council of chiefs. When the missionaries of the American Board arrived April 4, 1820, at Kailua Bay, Naihe and Kapiolani were among the first chiefs to welcome instruction and accept Christianity as far as they could understand it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Priests of Pele were numerous on the island Hawaii; women were among those of highest rank in that priesthood, and many of the personal followers of Kapiolani were worshippers. When Kapiolani said she was going to prove the falsity of the worship of Pele there was a storm of heartfelt opposition; the priests and worshippers of Pele honestly believed divine punishment would fall on her, and those who were Christians were afraid some awful explosion might overwhelm the company, as a large body of warriors had been destroyed thirty-four years before. When Kapiolani left her home in Kona her people, with great wailing, attempted to persuade her to stay; the grief, stimulated by fear of things supernatural, was uncontrollable, and the people followed their chiefess some distance with prayers and tears. For more than a hundred miles she journeyed, usually walking, sometimes having to cross miles of the roughest, most rugged and sharp-edged lava on the island Hawaii.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Toward the close of the day they crossed steaming cracks and chasms and drew nearer to the foul-smelling gaseous clouds of smoke which blew toward them from the great crater. Here a priestess of Pele of the highest rank came to meet the party and turn them away from the dominions of the fire-goddess unless they would offer appropriate sacrifices. This priestess was very haughty and bold, and forbade her to approach any nearer to the volcano on pain of death at the hands of the furious goddess Pele. 'Who are you?' asked Kapiolani. 'I am one in whom the God dwells.' 'If God dwells in you, then you are wise and can teach me. Come and sit down.' The priestess had seen printed pages or heard about them, so she drew out a piece of kapa and, saying that this was a letter from Pele, began to read or rather mumble an awful curse. The people with Kapiolani were hushed into a terrified silence, but she listened quietly until the priestess, carried beyond her depth, read a confused mass of jumbled words and unintelligible noises which she called the dialect of the ancient Pele. Then Kapiolani took her spelling-book, and a little book of a few printed hymns, and said: 'You have pretended to deliver a message from your god, but we have not understood it. Now I will read you a message which you can understand, for I, too, have a letter.' Then she read clearly the Biblical sentences printed in the spelling-book and some of the hymns; the priestess was silenced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kapiolani passed the priestess, went on to the crater, met Mr. Goodrich and was much affected by the effort he had made to aid her. Mr. Richards, a missionary, later wrote: 'Along the way to the volcano she was accosted by multitudes and entreated not to proceed. She answered, If I am destroyed, then you may all believe in Pele, but if I am not, you must all turn to the true writings.' Here in the large cones built up by leaping lava the natives said were the homes of the family of Pele; the roaring of the furnaces and crackling of flames was the music of drums beaten for the accompaniment of the household dances, and the red flaming surge was the surf wherein they played. Mr. Richards says: 'A man whose duty it was to feed Pele, by throwing berries and the like into the volcano, entreated her to go no farther. And what, said she, will be the harm? The man replied, You will die by Pele. Kapiolani answered, I shall not die by your god. That fire was kindled by my God. The man was silent and she went onward, descending several hundred feet, and there joined in a prayer to Jehovah. She also ate the berries consecrated to Pele, and threw stones into the volcano.' Bingham says: 'Then with the terrific bellowing and whizzing of the volcanic gases they mingled their voices in a solemn hymn of praise to the true God.' Alexander in the History of the Hawaiian People says, 'This has justly been called one of the greatest acts of moral courage ever performed.' Richards states that the leader of Kapiolani's party said to him: 'All the people of the district saw that she was not injured and have pronounced Pele to be powerless.' The influence of Kapiolani against this most influential form of idolatrous worship was felt throughout the whole nation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes, ch. 20 (1916), quoting Richards, Bingham and Alexander; not verbatim.

region.zh: 毛伊島考維基山丘（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (New York 1910)

summary.en: The heavens lay close on the earth; plants pushed them up inch by inch, and their leaves flattened forever. A man said to a woman: give me a drink from your gourd and I will push the heavens higher; drinking deep, Maui braced himself against the clouds, lifted them to the treetops, to the mountain summits, and thrust them into their place. A man who mocked the task was caught on the Lahaina coast and changed into a great black rock. Westervelt parallels the Samoa Tii-tii footprints, the serpent of Niue, and the Maori Tane straining sky from earth.
summary.zh: 昔日天穹低垂觸地；草木一寸寸頂天，葉片因此永遠攤平。一人向女子討水：『給我一口葫蘆水，我便把天舉高。』毛伊痛飲之後，抵住雲層奮力上舉——舉至樹梢、舉至山巔、終於撐定今日之位。譏笑者被追至拉海納海岸化作黑色巨石。桑加群島有蒂伊蒂伊六呎足印，紐埃島巨蛇碎身成島、血點為星，毛利人則說是塔內以足撐天——諸島同源。

sensitivity.note: Pacific-wide 'sky lifted' cluster; Westervelt's comparative notes summarized.

passages.text: Maui's home was for a long time enveloped by darkness. The heavens had fallen down, or, rather, had not been separated from the earth. According to some legends the skies pressed so closely and so heavily upon the earth that when the plants began to grow all the leaves were necessarily flat; according to other legends the plants had to push up the clouds a little, and thus caused the leaves to flatten out into larger surface so that they could better drive the skies back and hold them in place. Thus the leaves became flat at first and have so remained through all the days of mankind. The plants lifted the sky inch by inch until men were able to crawl about between the heavens and the earth, and thus pass from place to place and visit one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long time, according to the Hawaiian legends, a man, supposed to be Maui, came to a woman and said: 'Give me a drink from your gourd calabash, and I will push the heavens higher.' The woman handed the gourd to him; when he had taken a deep draught he braced himself against the clouds and lifted them to the height of the trees; again he hoisted the sky and carried it to the tops of the mountains; then with great exertion he thrust it upwards once more and pressed it to the place it now occupies. Nevertheless dark clouds many times hang low along the eastern slope of Maui's great mountain, Haleakala, and descend in heavy rains upon the hill Kauwiki; but they dare not stay, lest Maui the strong come and hurl them so far away that they cannot come back again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man who had been watching the process of lifting the sky ridiculed Maui for attempting such a difficult task; when the clouds rested on the tops of the mountains Maui turned to punish his critic. The man had fled to the other side of the island; Maui rapidly pursued and finally caught him on the sea coast, not many miles north of the town now known as Lahaina; after a brief struggle the man was changed into a great black rock which can be seen by any traveler who desires to localize the legends of Hawaii. In Samoa Tii-tii is the name of the one who braced his feet against the rocks and pushed the sky up; the foot-prints, some six feet long, are said to be shown by the natives. One of the Ellice group, Niu Island, says that as the serpent began to lift the sky the people clapped their hands and shouted 'Lift up! High! Higher!' but the body of the serpent finally broke into pieces which became islands, and the blood sprinkled its drops on the sky and became stars. The New Zealand Maoris say the six sons of heaven and earth discussed separating their parents; Rongo attempted to lift the sky but could not tear it from the earth, then Tangaroa failed, then Haumia and Tu struggled in vain; but Tane, the father of giant forests, pushed and lifted until he thrust the sky far up above him, and they discovered their descendants, the multitude of human beings concealed and crushed by the clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 3 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Maui Smites the Long Eel Tuna-roa

region.zh: 考伊基附近河岸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian and New Zealand oral traditions; retold 1910 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (New York 1910)

summary.en: Maui's wife Hina-a-te-lepo, drawing water at the river bank, is twice struck down and befouled by the tail of Tuna-roa, the long eel. Maui digs the 'sacred digging', a tabu ditch, across which he stretches a net, chants rain down, and floods the eel out of his deep pool; with his stone axe Ma-Tori-Tori, 'the severer', he cuts off the head and pieces the body. The tail becomes the conger-eel, the fresh-water parts the common eels, the head-hairs vines and creepers, and drops of blood mark birds red and make certain trees red-wooded - and from that day Maui's children eat eels freely.
summary.zh: 毛伊之妻希娜阿泰萊波河邊汲水，兩遭長鰻圖納羅阿尾擊、遍染黏污。毛伊掘『神聖之溝』——一條僅為擒鰻而設的禁溝——架網於上，誦咒召雨，洪水沖開深潭，將巨鰻沖入網中。他以石斧『瑪托里托里——斷絕者』一擊斷其首，碎其身：尾成大海鰻，淡水之部成尋常鰻，髮絲化藤蔓，血點染鳥羽成紅斑、入樹則木材盡赤——自此毛伊子孫恣食鰻魚。

passages.text: Maui sought Hina-a-te-lepo, daughter of the swamp, and secured her as his wife; she cared for his thatched house as any other Polynesian woman was in the habit of doing, and attempted the hurried task of cooking his food before he snared the sun and gave her sufficient daylight for her labors. They lived near the bank of a river from which Hina was in the habit of bringing water for the household needs. One day she went down to the stream with her calabash, entwined with wreaths of leaves and flowers as was the custom among Polynesian women; while she was standing on the bank, Tuna-roa, the long eel, saw her. He swam up to the bank and suddenly struck her and knocked her into the water and covered her with slime from the blow given by his tail. Hina escaped and returned to her home, saying nothing to Maui about the trouble; but the next day, while getting water, she was again overthrown and befouled by the slime of Tuna-roa. Then Hina became angry and reported the trouble to Maui, who decided to punish the long eel and started out to find his hiding place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of the New Zealand legends as collected by White state that Tuna-roa was a very smooth-skinned chief who lived on the opposite bank of the stream and, seeing Hina, had insulted her; when Maui saw this chief he caught two pieces of wood over which he was accustomed to slide his canoe into the sea, carried them to the stream and laid them from bank to bank as a bridge over which he might entice Tuna-roa to cross. Maui took his stone axe Ma-Tori-Tori, the severer, and concealed himself near the bank; when the long eel had crossed the stream Maui rushed out and killed him with a mighty blow of the stone axe, cutting the head from the body. Other legends say that Maui found Tuna-roa living as an eel in a deep water hole in a swamp on the sea-coast, or in the river near Maui's home; he saw that he could not get at his enemy without letting off the water which protected him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Therefore into the forest went Maui, and with sacred ceremonies selected trees from the wood of which he prepared tools and weapons. Meanwhile, in addition to the insult given to Hina, Tuna-roa had caught and devoured two of Maui's children, which made Maui more determined to kill him. Maui made the narrow spade and the sharp spears with which to pierce either the earth or his enemy, consecrating them to the work of preparing a ditch by which to draw off the water protecting the long eel. The work of trench-making was accomplished with many incantations and prayers; the ditch was named the sacred digging, and was tabooed to all other purposes except that of catching Tuna-roa. Across this ditch Maui stretched a strong net, and then began a new series of chants and ceremonies to bring down an abundance of rain; soon the flood came and the overflowing waters rushed down the sacred ditch, the walls of the deep pool gave way and the long eel was carried down the trench into the waiting net. Then there was commotion - Tuna-roa was struggling for freedom. Maui saw him and hastened to grasp his stone axe, the severer; hurrying to the net he struck Tuna-roa a terrible blow and cut off the head; with a few more blows he cut the body in pieces. The head and tail were carried out into the sea: the head became fish and the tail became the great conger-eel; other parts of the body became sea monsters, but some parts which fell in fresh water became the common eels; from the hairs of the head came certain vines and creepers among the plants. After the death of Tuna-roa the offspring of Maui were in no danger of being killed and soon multiplied into a large family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another New Zealand legend related by White says that Maui built a sliding place of logs over which Tuna-roa must pass when coming from the river, and made a screen behind which he could secrete himself while watching; he commanded Hina to come down to the river and wait on the bank to attract Tuna-roa. Soon the long eel was seen in the water swimming near to Hina; she went to a place back of the logs which Maui had laid down, and Tuna-roa came towards her and began to slide down the skids. Maui sprang out from his hiding place and killed Tuna-roa with his axe and cut him in pieces; the tail became the conger-eel, parts of his body became fresh-water eels; some of the blood fell upon birds and always after marked them with red spots, some was thrown into certain trees making this wood always red, and the muscles became vines and creepers. From this time the children of Maui caught and ate the eels of both salt and fresh water; eel traps were made, and Maui taught the people the proper chants or incantations to use when catching eels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 7 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Hina-uri's Death Song and Chief Tini-rau
title.zh: 希娜烏里葬歌與酋長蒂尼勞

region.en: Sea drift from Aotearoa to Tini-rau's isle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自紐西蘭漂流至蒂尼勞之島（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (New York 1910)

summary.en: A New Zealand variant of the Irawaru cycle: Maui changes the brother-in-law into a dog by incantation while cleaning his hair in sleep. Hina-uri sings her death song to the steep billows and the ocean god, casts herself into the sea, and drifts many moons until two fishermen warm her body back to life; chief Tini-rau takes her as a wife, but his jealous other wives drive her away - the opening of the Tinirau cycle cut also from Grey's Rupe chapter.
summary.zh: 紐西蘭變體：毛伊趁替連襟理髮催眠之機施咒，將其化為犬。希娜烏里唱著葬歌向滔天巨浪與海神告別，投身大海，漂流多個月相，終被漁夫救起、以火溫暖還陽。酋長蒂尼勞娶她為妻；眾妒婦不容，將其逐出——此即蒂尼勞傳說之開端（另見魯佩篇）。

sensitivity.note: Variant record linking Grey's Hinauri/Ihungarupaea record and the Maori dog-cycle.

passages.text: The Tahu and Hau tribes of New Zealand tell a different story: Maui went to visit Ira-waru; together they set out on a journey. After a time they rested by the wayside and became sleepy. Maui asked Ira-waru to cleanse his head; this gave him the restful, soothing touch which aided sleep. Then Maui proposed that Ira-waru sleep, and taking the head in his hands put his brother-in-law to sleep; then by incantations he made the sleep very deep and prolonged. Meanwhile he pulled the ears and arms and limbs until they were properly lengthened; he drew out the under jaw until it had the form of a dog's mouth; he stretched the end of the backbone into a tail, and then wakened Ira-waru and drove him back when he tried to follow the path to the settlement. Hina-uri went out and called her husband; he came to her, leaping and barking; she decided that this was her husband, and in her agony reproached Maui and wandered away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Hina-uri saw the state of her husband she went into the thatched house by which Ira-waru had so often stood watching the hollow log in which she dried the fish and preserved the birds speared in the mountains. She bound her girdle and hala-leaf apron around her and went down to the sea to drown herself, that her body might be eaten by the monsters of the sea. When she came to the shell-covered beach she sat down and sang her death song: 'I weep, I call to the steep billows of the sea and to him, the great, the ocean god; to monsters, all now hidden, to come and bury me, who now am wrapped in mourning. Let the waves wear their mourning, too, and sleep as sleeps the dead.' Then Hina-uri threw herself into the sea and was borne on the waves many moons, at last drifting to shore, to be found by two fishermen. They carried the body off to the fire and warmed it back to life; they brushed off the sea moss and sea weeds and rubbed her until she awoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon they told their chief, Tini-rau, what a beautiful woman they had found in the sea. He came and took her away to make her one of his wives. But the other wives were jealous and drove Hina-uri away from the chief's houses - the opening of the Tinirau cycle of New Zealand legend, in which Rupe's descent to find his lost sister and the death of Kae in the house of Tinirau are told at length.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 8 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Maui's Kite and the Winds of Waipio
title.zh: 毛伊放鳶與懷皮奧之風

region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛懷盧庫河

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (New York 1910)

summary.en: Only Hawaiian myth gives kite-flying to a god. Maui builds a kite larger than any house, of kapa on a line of olona fibre, and calls the imprisoned winds from the calabash of the priest Kaleiioku in Waipio - 'O winds, winds of Waipio, come quickly, come with power'. The winds climb the heavens and attack the monster kite; the strain builds until the line breaks and the kite is tossed across the island to Kau. Leaping the mountains in half a dozen strides, Maui fetches it back - 'Maui the Swift' - and ever after the kite's floating means dry weather for drying kapa.
summary.zh: 夏威夷神話獨有：諸神亦放紙鳶。毛伊製巨鳶大於屋宇，以卡帕布為體、奧洛納纖維為線，召喚被囚於懷皮奧祭司卡萊伊奧庫風葫蘆中的群風——『懷皮奧之風啊，快來，挾威而來！』群風攀天撲擊巨鳶；線繃至極而斷，鳶被拋過全島落於考烏。毛伊六步跨越高山取回——人稱『飛毛腿毛伊』——從此鳶在，則天晴，百姓攤卡帕曬布，歡呼『毛伊的鳶在天上』。

sensitivity.note: Kite-weather etiology; petrified canoe and fishhook landmarks noted.

passages.text: The Hawaiian myths are perhaps the only ones of the Pacific Ocean which give to any of the gods the pleasure and excitement of kite flying. Maui, after repeated experiments, made a large kite for himself; it was much larger than any house of his time or generation. He twisted a long line from the strong fibers of the native plant known as the olona; he endowed both kite and string with marvelous powers and launched the kite up toward the clouds. It rose very slowly; the winds were not lifting it into the sky. Maui remembered that an old priest lived in Waipio valley, the largest and finest valley of the large island, Hawaii, on which he made his home. This priest had a covered calabash in which he compelled the winds to hide when he did not wish them to play on land and sea; the priest's name was Kaleiioku, and his calabash was known as ipu-makani-a ka maumau, the calabash of the perpetual winds. Maui called for the priest who had charge of the winds to open his calabash and let them come up to Hilo and blow along the Wailuku river; the natives say that the place where Maui stood was marked by the pressure of his feet in the lava rocks of the river bank as he braced himself to hold the kite against the increasing force of the winds which pushed it towards the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the priest lifted the cover of the calabash of the winds and let the strong winds of Hilo escape; along the sea coast they rushed until as they entered Hilo Bay they heard the voice of Maui calling - 'O winds, winds of Hilo, hasten and come to me.' With a tumultuous rush the strong winds turned toward the mountains; they forced their way along the gorges and palisades of the Wailuku river; they leaped into the heavens, making a fierce attack upon the monster which Maui had sent into the sky. The kite struggled as it was pushed upward by the hands of the fierce winds, but Maui rejoiced; his heart was uplifted by the joy of the conflict in which his strength to hold was pitted against the power of the winds to tear away. The kite had been made of the strongest kapa which Maui's mother could prepare; it was not torn, although it was bent backward to its utmost limit. Then the strain came on the strong cord of olona fibre; the line was stretched and strained as the kite was pushed back. Then Maui called again and again for stronger winds to come; the cord was drawn out until the kite was far above the mountains; at last it broke and the kite was tossed over the craters of the volcanoes to the land of the district of Kau on the other side of the island. Then Maui was angry and hastily leaped over the mountains, which are nearly fourteen thousand feet in altitude; in a half dozen strides he had crossed the fifty or sixty miles from his home to the place where the kite lay - his name was Maui-Mama, Maui the Swift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Maui returned with his kite he was more careful in calling the winds to aid him in his sport. The people watched their wise neighbor and soon learned that the kite could be a great blessing to them: when it was soaring in the sky there was always dry and pleasant weather; it was a day for great rejoicing; they could spread out their kapa cloth to dry as long as the kite was in the sky; they could carry out their necessary work without fear of the rain. Therefore when any one saw the kite beginning to float along the mountain side he would call out joyfully, 'E! Maui's kite is in the heavens.' Maui would send his kite into the blue sky and then tie the line to the great black stones in the bed of the Wailuku river. Time passed, and even the demi-god died; the fish hook with which he drew the Hawaiian Islands up from the depths of the sea was allowed to lie on the lava by the Wailuku river until it became a part of the stone; the double canoe was carried far inland and then permitted to petrify by the river side; the two stones which represent the double canoe now bear the name Waa-Kauhi, and the kite has fallen from the sky far up on the mountain side, where it still rests, a flat plot of rich land between Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 9 (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Hina of Hilo Beats Her Tapa by the Falls

region.en: Wailuku river falls, Hilo, Hawaii Island
region.zh: 夏威夷島希洛懷盧庫河瀑布

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (New York 1910)

summary.en: The Hina of Hilo is the true legendary Hina of all Polynesia, her stories transplanted by settlers to Hilo. In a cave under one of the Wailuku falls she pounded tapa with chants and incantations - round clubs and four-sided mallets, bark soaked and beaten day after day into sheets soft as silk. Days too short for drying, she grieved until Maui snared the sun for her. Her southern sisters beat out the glistening clouds: thunder when she throws aside the stones that hold them, lightning leaping from sheet to sheet.
summary.zh: 希洛的希娜即全波利尼西亞共尊的希娜女神；移民攜其傳說落籍希洛。她在懷盧庫瀑布下的岩穴中槌打樹皮布——浸皮、圓槌、方槌，伴著咒歌，日復一日捶出柔若絲綢的卡帕。日光太短、布無法晾乾，她鬱鬱寡歡，直到毛伊為她擒住太陽。南太平洋的姊妹希娜則在天上槌雲成布：擲開鎮布之石便是雷，雲層間閃跳之光便是電。

sensitivity.note: Moon-goddess Hina record; links to the kapa-origin and thunder-stone myths.

passages.text: Hina is not an uncommon name in Hawaiian genealogies; it is usually accompanied by some adjective which explains or identifies the person. In Hawaii the name Hina is feminine; this is also true throughout all Polynesia. The Hina of Hilo is the same as the goddess of that name most widely known throughout Polynesia - and yet her legends are located by the ancient Hawaiians in Hilo, as if that place were her only home; the legends are so old that the Hawaiians have forgotten their origin in other lands, and the stories were brought with the immigrants who settled on the Hilo coast, finding their final location with the families who brought them. There are three Hawaiian Hinas practically distinct from each other, although a supernatural element is connected with each one: Hina who was stolen from Hawaii by a chief of Molokai was an historical character; another Hina, the wife of Kuula, the fish god, was pre-eminently a local deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wailuku river, which flows through the town of Hilo, is a series of waterfalls and rapids following the course of an ancient lava flow, sometimes forcing its way under bridges of lava, thus forming boiling pots, and sometimes pouring in massive sheets over the edges of precipices. By the side of this river Hina's son Maui had his lands. In the very bed of the river, in a cave under one of the largest falls, Hina made her own home, concealed from the world by the silver veil of falling water and lulled to sleep by the continual roar of the flood falling into the deep pool below. By the side of this river she pounded her tapa and prepared her food; here were the small graceful mamake and the coarser wauke trees from which the bark was stripped. The days were very short and there was no time for rest while making tapa cloth; as soon as the morning light reddened the clouds Hina would take her calabash filled with water and her little bundle of round clubs and her four-sided mallets and hasten to the sacred spot where, with chants and incantations, the tapa was made. Beautiful tapa, soft as silk, was made by adding pulpy mass to pulpy mass and beating it day after day until the fibres were lost and a sheet of close-woven bark cloth was formed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Hina of Hilo was grieved as she toiled because after she had pounded the sheets out so thin that they were ready to be dried she found it almost impossible to secure the necessary aid of the sun in the drying process; she would rise as soon as she could see and hasten to spread her tapa - until Maui snared the sun for her. The legends of the Southern Pacific Islands show more imagination: they say that Ina (Hina) was such a wonderful artist in making beautiful tapas that she was placed in the skies, where she beats out glistening fine tapas, the white and glorious clouds. When she stretches these cloud sheets out to dry she places stones along the edges, so that the fierce winds of the heavens shall not blow them away; when she throws these stones aside, the skies reverberate with thunder; when she rolls her cloud sheets of tapa together, the folds glisten with flashes of light and lightning leaps from sheet to sheet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Legends of Ma-ui, ch. 12 (1910); not verbatim.
